item.title: Stored energy and mechanical load in deformable dielectrics: What the macroscopic fields determine
item.description: arXiv:2611.30347v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The mechanical load that an electric field exerts inside a deformable dielectric has been debated since Kelvin derived it from forces on dipoles and Helmholtz from an energy variation. Current electroelastic models follow the energy route, with the stored energy and its deformation dependence as constitutive input. Using a classical model of ions, electrons, and their fields and spatial averaging, we examine what this energy represents and how much of it the macroscopic fields determine. The macroscopic fields carry only their own energy. In their balance, $\mathbf J_{\rm total}\cdot\mathbf E$ is power leaving them; they do not show where it goes. In the model this power feeds carrier motion and field structure that averaging removes. For linear reversible response its time integral is $\tfrac12\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf P$: $\tfrac12\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D$ is the macroscopic-field energy $\tfrac12\varepsilon_0|\mathbf E|^2$ plus recoverable energy of this structure. Thermal, kinetic, and elastic energies follow likewise, giving one energy map across thermodynamics, mechanics, and electrodynamics. Under deformation the same exchange supplies mechanical work; the fields fix the total, not its division between work and stored energy. We formulate a sufficiency criterion: a macroscopic description determines the load when all microstructures consistent with it give the same virtual work for the deformations of interest. For linear, nonlinear, and hysteretic response we specify the material information required; the linear case recovers the Helmholtz stress. Two dipole arrays with identical macroscopic fields, previously found to differ in boundary traction, show that sufficiency can fail; the criterion separates cases where constitutive data suffice from those needing interface or microstructural detail.
item.dc:creator: Bela Schulte Westhoff

item.title: Quantum aspects of the classical Maxwell's equations in free space from the perspective of the generalised correspondence principle
item.description: arXiv:2509.02620v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Due to the advent of Quantum Mechanics' 100th anniversary in 2025, we wrote this review paper in order to present a discussion that addresses the foundations of this theory. And since the creation of this Mechanics and other quantum theories was guided, for instance, by correspondence principles that needed to be identified between them and other well-established physical theories, this paper will be devoted to discussing the correspondence between Quantum Mechanics and Maxwell's theory of electromagnetism. More precisely, what we will do throughout this paper is discuss how the Maxwell's electromagnetic theory in free space and the generalised formulation of the correspondence principle already pointed, together, to the basis of a Quantum Mechanics that would only be formulated half a century later. And, in order to make this very clear, we will show that the quantum-mechanical description of a photon can already be identified, simply, by manipulating Maxwell's equations in free space with mathematical resources that, for instance, were already well known before the advent of Quantum Mechanics.
item.dc:creator: M. F. Araujo de Resende, Leonardo S. F. Santos, R. Albertini Silva

item.title: Newton's Second Law: A Structural Necessity of Mechanics Constrained by Excluded Perpetual Motion and Universal Free Fall
item.description: arXiv:2608.06266v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: For over three centuries, Newton's second law (F = ma) has governed mechanics with extraordinary success, while its epistemic warrant has remained empirical. That merely empirical contingency vanishes once mechanics is constrained by two principles: the principle of excluded perpetual motion (PEPM) with its pre-Newtonian phenomenological content and the weak equivalence principle (WEP) with universal free fall as its primitive content. The PEPM secures the applicability of Suppes' measurement-theoretic framework to gravitational mass and force, exposing the formal structure latent in their empirical manifestations and establishing both as independent primitives. Gravity bridges statics and kinematics in Stevin's and Galileo's inclined-plane arguments, where the common sine factor in force and acceleration cancels in F/a. Cycle arguments under the PEPM extend this result to arbitrary force mechanisms, establishing F/a as object-intrinsic and securing inertial mass as a well-defined physical quantity. Further constrained by universal free fall, the resulting quantitative structure compels the equivalence of inertial and gravitational mass, with Newton's second law as the operational expression of that equivalence. Direct implications include constraints on modified-inertia MOND that follow from the PEPM alone. The PEPM also places free-fall and torsion-balance experiments on equal footing as tests of the WEP. Together with the WEP, the derivation further grounds both the dimensional reduction of mechanics and the location-invariance of the Kibble-balance realization of the SI kilogram. Deeper still, Newton's second law derives its necessity from exclusion and invariance principles whose scope extends beyond mechanics itself.
item.dc:creator: Lars Nordmann

item.title: Relative periodic orbits of a free spinning loop
item.description: arXiv:2611.23582v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A closed elastic string with no external forces can hold any shape while its material moves steadily along the curve (a steady axial motion), because its tension and the force needed to turn the material around a bend are both proportional to the curvature. I compute the periodic motions that grow from the simplest of these motions, the spinning ring, by Newton's method on a chain of masses. They include rotating waves that turn at twice the rotation rate of the material, standing "flappers" with two to five lobes, and period-doubled and period-tripled orbits. The chain only approximates the string. The orbits and their strong instabilities change little with more masses and are properties of the continuous string. Most weak instabilities change with the number of masses and are artifacts of approximating the string by a finite chain. The saddle flapper of a loop stretched 30% beyond its natural length is neutrally stable at small heights and unstable at large ones. Near a stretch of 1/12 the saddle flapper resonates with the breathing of the ring. Below that stretch the flapper slows as it grows and above it the flapper speeds up, and near the resonance two families of saddle flappers overlap. An unstable saddle flapper trades energy back and forth with an in-plane oval, and at large amplitude the energy spreads to the shortest waves of the chain. For Keller's linear string, whose tension is proportional to the stretched length, every motion is periodic, and every knot carries an exactly periodic flapper. For a Hookean string the curvature of a knot couples a ripple to stretching waves that travel at a different speed, and in the simulations a ripple on a sliding knot does not return to its starting shape. Whether a Hookean knot carries any periodic flapper is open.
item.dc:creator: Nicholas B. Tufillaro

item.title: A time-domain adversarial example demonstrating the failure of $H^1$ elements in $a$-$\phi$ electromagnetic simulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.26546v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Frequently, $H^1$ continuous finite elements are used in computational electromagnetics despite it being widely known that such an interpolation is not guaranteed to furnish reliable approximations of solutions to general initial/boundary value problems. It is mathematically more natural to use $H(\text{Curl})$ elements (edge elements) than $H^1$ elements, since the former form part of a discrete complex that respects the differential-geometric structure of Maxwell's equations while the latter do not. However, most work discussing the failure of $H^1$ elements for electromagnetics is esoteric and concrete examples demonstrating the clear advantage of edge elements are generally restricted to quasi-static, frequency-domain, or eigenvalue problems. In this work, we summarize essential facts regarding $H^1$ and $H(\text{Curl})$ elements and present a physically feasible yet intentionally adversarial time-domain eddy-current example demonstrating the failure of gauge-penalized $H^1$ elements in an $a$-$\phi$ formulation compared to explicit gauge-free mixed scalar/edge $H^1/H(\text{Curl})$ elements. The results indicate that edge elements can be used to furnish reasonable results for general loading conditions, whereas penalized $H^1$ elements fail (e.g., converge to an incorrect state) even with mesh refinement.
item.dc:creator: Timothy Carlson, Sanjay Govindjee
